ai-at-work.title: TechCrunch Mobility: The AI skills arms race is coming for automotive
ai-at-work.excerpt: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility — your central hub for news and insights on the future of transportation.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: The automotive industry is scrambling to hire AI talent as companies recognize that software and AI expertise now matter more than traditional car-building skills. This matters to digital workplace leaders because it signals a broader talent crunch hitting every sector: the competition for AI-capable people is only getting fiercer, and your retention strategies need to account for it. Here's the thing though: if the auto industry wanted to keep their engineers, maybe they should have started treating software development like a first-class concern instead of an afterthought back in 2015.

ai-at-work.title: The haves and have nots of the AI gold rush
ai-at-work.excerpt: The vibes around the current AI boom aren't great, even in the tech industry.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Companies are dividing into those with the resources to implement AI effectively and those left behind without the budget or expertise to catch up. This matters because your organization's competitive position in hiring talent, automating workflows, and solving real business problems is increasingly tied to AI capabilities you either have or don't. The uncomfortable truth is that the "AI gold rush" is really just widening the gap between well-funded enterprises and everyone else, which means mid-market companies need to stop chasing shiny demos and start figuring out which AI investments actually move the needle for their specific problems.

ai-at-work.title: Research repository ArXiv will ban authors for a year if they let AI do all the work
ai-at-work.excerpt: ArXiv is doing more to crack down on the careless use of large language models in scientific papers.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: ArXiv announced it will temporarily ban researchers who use AI to generate entire papers without meaningful human contribution. This matters because it signals that even in tech-forward communities, there's a hard line between using AI as a tool and abdicating actual work. Look, we can debate AI's role in the workplace all day, but let's be honest: if a research repository has to ban laziness, your organization definitely needs clearer AI governance policies before someone submits a "strategic initiative" that ChatGPT wrote in five minutes.

ai-at-work.title: Railway secures $100 million to challenge AWS with AI-native cloud infrastructure
ai-at-work.excerpt: Railway, a San Francisco-based cloud platform that has quietly amassed two million developers without spending a dollar on marketing, announced Thursday that it raised $100 million in a Series B fundi
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Railway just raised $100 million to build cloud infrastructure purpose-built for AI workloads, positioning itself as an alternative to AWS and other legacy platforms. This matters because your organization's AI ambitions are probably already hitting friction with infrastructure designed for the last decade of computing patterns. Honestly, watching another startup promise to "disrupt" cloud while AWS prints money is entertaining, but Railway's quiet two million developer base suggests they might actually be building something people want rather than just talking about it.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft’s Patch Tuesday updates: Keeping up with the latest fixes
tools-tech.excerpt: Long before Taco Tuesday became part of the pop-culture vernacular, Tuesdays were synonymous with security — and for anyone in the tech world, they still are. Patch Tuesday, as you most likely know, r
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft releases security patches on the second Tuesday of every month across its entire product portfolio, a practice that's been standard for over two decades. Digital workplace pros need to understand their patch management cadence because unpatched systems are open doors for ransomware and data breaches that will absolutely ruin your month. The real trick isn't knowing when patches drop, it's actually testing and deploying them before someone in your organization clicks on the wrong email and turns your network into someone else's playground.

tools-tech.title: For May, Patch Tuesday means 139 updates —  but no zero-days
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft this week released 139 updates affecting Windows, Office, .NET, and SQL Server (though there were no updates for Microsoft Exchange Server). Despite the absence of zero-days, the May Patch T
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft dropped 139 patches in May with no zero-day exploits, though three unauthenticated network RCEs in Windows and Office still earned "Patch Now" ratings. This matters because your users are running these vulnerable services right now, and threat actors absolutely know about these flaws the moment patches drop. Look, 139 updates sounds like a lot until you realize it's just another Tuesday in the Microsoft ecosystem, so stop acting surprised and get your testing and deployment process dialed in because this is the baseline, not the exception.

tools-tech.title: Here’s one career emerging from the AI shift: ‘forward-deployed engineers’
tools-tech.excerpt: On Thursday, Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian issued a call for “forward-deployed engineers” to apply for jobs in the company’s go-to-market AI team. Their task: help non-tech organizations scale up the
tools-tech.dwp_take: Google is hiring "forward-deployed engineers" to help non-tech companies actually implement AI instead of just talking about it. This matters because your organization probably has AI projects stuck in pilot purgatory, and you'll need people who can bridge the gap between what vendors promise and what actually works in your messy, real-world environment. Finally, a job title that admits implementation is harder than PowerPoint slides, which is refreshingly honest for the tech industry.

tools-tech.title: Why Apple needs Intel — and America needs them both
tools-tech.excerpt: If you think about it, it’s in the national interest for Apple to work with Intel to develop at least some capacity for silicon production outside of Taiwan. It’s also in Apple’s interest, as its cont
tools-tech.dwp_take: Apple is apparently reconsidering its complete abandonment of Intel chips because geopolitical supply chain risks and production capacity constraints are making Taiwan-dependent manufacturing look riskier than it did five years ago. This matters to digital workplace leaders because your device refresh cycles, support costs, and ecosystem planning are all hostage to semiconductor supply chains that nobody actually controls. Here's the thing though: if Apple needed Intel's help to solve this problem, Intel's current state must be pretty dire, which tells you everything you need to know about where American chip manufacturing actually stands today.

digital-culture.title: 5 ways constraints boost productivity and creativity at work
digital-culture.excerpt: Below, David Epstein shares five key insights from his new book, Inside the Box: How Constraints Make Us Better. David is the author of The New York Times bestsellers Range and The Sports Gene. He has
digital-culture.dwp_take: A researcher named David Epstein wrote a book arguing that constraints actually make teams more productive and creative, not less. This matters because most digital workplace leaders spend their time removing friction and adding tools, when sometimes the opposite approach works better. The irony is thick: we've spent three decades building unlimited options and infinite cloud storage, and it turns out people do better work when you tell them no.

digital-culture.title: Dropbox chief people officer: The hybrid work model is ‘the worst of all worlds’
digital-culture.excerpt: As companies battle it out with employees over RTO policies, Dropbox is choosing to stay out of the drama by prioritizing remote work. “The pandemic tested our assumption that we have to be in person
digital-culture.dwp_take: Dropbox ditched hybrid work entirely and went all-in on remote, with their chief people officer calling hybrid the worst of both worlds. This matters because while most companies are still wrestling with RTO mandates and hybrid schedules, Dropbox's move shows that picking a lane and committing to it actually works better than the awkward middle ground. The irony here is thick: a file-sharing company had to learn what the rest of us are still figuring out, which is that remote-first beats the worst-of-both-worlds compromise every single time.

digital-culture.title: Why being good at your job isn’t enough to get promoted anymore
digital-culture.excerpt: If you’ve been in the corporate world long enough, you might have seen technical specialists hit a career ceiling. They’re brilliant at what they do, but they can struggle to advance to leadership pos
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company says technical specialists often plateau in their careers because management requires big-picture thinking rather than task expertise. This matters to digital workplace pros because it means your infrastructure experts and security specialists won't naturally evolve into leaders without deliberate development in strategic communication and organizational thinking. Here's the thing though: companies that force their best technical people into management roles they never wanted are shooting themselves in the foot, so maybe the real answer is creating genuine technical leadership tracks instead of pretending everyone wants to manage people.

industry-news.title: Revamped Colorado AI law targets ‘consequential’ HR decisions, takes effect in 2027
industry-news.excerpt: After scrapping a version challenged in court, the state wants its second attempt to be “a model for the rest of the country,” Gov. Jared Polis said.
industry-news.dwp_take: Colorado passed a revised AI law that focuses on "consequential" HR decisions and won't take effect until 2027, giving companies time to prepare. This matters because it's the first serious state-level regulation of AI in hiring and employment, and other states are definitely watching to see what sticks legally. Honestly, the three-year runway is both generous and telling: even the governor knows companies will need that long to figure out what "consequential" actually means in practice.

industry-news.title: EEOC: Walmart settles ADA lawsuit alleging deaf applicant was denied ASL interpreter
industry-news.excerpt: Under a two-year consent decree, Walmart must pay the applicant $230,000 and post a list of ASL interpreters for managers and employees involved in the hiring process.
industry-news.dwp_take: Walmart just got hit with a $230,000 settlement and a two-year consent decree for denying an ASL interpreter to a deaf job applicant, which means they now have to maintain interpreter lists for hiring managers. This matters because your hiring process is part of your digital workplace, and if your applicant tracking system, interview platforms, or onboarding workflows don't account for accessibility needs, you're setting yourself up for the same legal and financial headache. Here's the thing: accessibility isn't a compliance checkbox you tick once and forget, it's an ongoing practice that requires actual coordination between HR, IT, and facilities to work properly.

industry-news.title: What puts organizations at risk of losing AI talent?
industry-news.excerpt: “AI adoption is a culture issue, not just a training issue,” a Gartner report said.
industry-news.dwp_take: Organizations are struggling to retain AI talent because they're treating adoption as a skills problem when the real bottleneck is organizational culture and leadership buy-in. This matters because your best AI people will walk if they're stuck in teams where leadership doesn't actually want to change how work gets done. Here's the thing: you can't train your way out of a culture problem, and no amount of LinkedIn Learning courses will convince a talented engineer to stick around while executives ignore their recommendations.

industry-news.title: Entry-level productivity expectations have increased due to AI, report says
industry-news.excerpt: Nearly a third of HR professionals told D2L they’re hiring fewer early career workers and using artificial intelligence to fill in the gaps.
industry-news.dwp_take: A third of HR pros are hiring fewer entry-level workers and leaning on AI to do the job instead. This matters because it directly impacts your digital workplace strategy: you're building tools and processes for a smaller, more senior workforce, which changes everything about training, collaboration, and knowledge transfer. The irony is that by cutting junior staff, companies are actually making their AI implementation harder since nobody's around anymore to do the unglamorous work of teaching machines what actually matters in your business.
